title: Earth, the Solar System, Stars & the Universe
description: Day and night, seasons and Moon phases; the Solar System and the accretion model; gravity on other planets; light-travel times; orbital motion; the life cycle of stars; and the redshift and microwave evidence for the expanding Universe (IGCSE 0625).

notes.heading: Day, Night and the Seasons
notes.body:
📌 Definitions
The **Earth rotates on its axis once in approximately 24 hours** — this rotation causes day and night, as each place on the surface turns to face the Sun (day) and then away from it (night). The **Earth orbits the Sun once in approximately 365 days** — one year.

🔑 How it works — seasons
Earth's axis is **tilted** relative to its orbit around the Sun. As Earth travels round its orbit, each hemisphere takes turns being tilted **towards** the Sun and **away** from it:
• Tilted towards the Sun: sunlight strikes the surface more directly (closer to overhead) and days are longer — **summer**. More solar energy arrives per square metre.
• Tilted away: sunlight arrives at a slanting angle and days are shorter — **winter**.
• The two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same moment.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying summer happens because Earth is CLOSER to the Sun. The orbit is nearly circular; the tilt, not the distance, causes the seasons — and it explains why the hemispheres are in opposite seasons, which a distance change could not.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Rotation (24 h) → day/night. Orbit (365 d) + axial tilt → seasons.
• The Sun does not orbit the Earth — the daily motion of the Sun across the sky is the Earth's rotation seen from the surface.

notes.heading: The Moon
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The **Moon orbits the Earth approximately once a month** (about 27.3 days, and about 29.5 days for the full cycle of phases). The Moon is a natural satellite; it shines only by **reflecting sunlight** — it produces no light of its own.

🔑 How it works — phases
As the Moon orbits, we see different fractions of its sunlit half:
• **New Moon** — the sunlit half faces away from us; the Moon appears dark.
• **Crescent → first quarter → gibbous** — a growing (waxing) sliver of the lit side becomes visible.
• **Full Moon** — the whole Earth-facing side is sunlit.
• Then the cycle wanes back to new. One complete cycle takes about a month — the origin of the word "month".

💡 Worked Example
If the Moon is full on 3 March, the next full Moon is about a month later, in early April, and a half-lit first-quarter Moon occurs about a week after new Moon.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Thinking Earth's shadow causes the phases. Phases are just our changing view of the half of the Moon that the Sun illuminates; an eclipse of the Moon (Earth's shadow) is a separate, much rarer event.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Moon orbits Earth ≈ once a month; Earth orbits Sun ≈ 365 days; Earth rotates ≈ 24 hours — the three timescales are a favourite exam recall set.

notes.heading: The Solar System and the Accretion Model
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The **Solar System** consists of one star — the **Sun**, which contains almost all of its mass — plus **eight planets** with their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets, all held in orbit by the Sun's gravity.

🔑 How it works — structure
• Four small, **rocky inner planets** (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) orbit closest to the Sun.
• Four large **gaseous outer planets** (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) orbit further out.
• The **asteroid belt** lies between Mars and Jupiter; **comets** follow long, highly elliptical orbits.
• The Sun is a medium-sized star, composed mostly of hydrogen and helium, radiating energy released by nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core.

🔑 How it works — the accretion model of formation
The Solar System formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust (a **nebula**):
1. Gravity pulled the cloud together; the collapsing centre heated up and became the **protostar** that grew into the Sun.
2. The rest of the cloud flattened into a rotating **accretion disc** around the young Sun.
3. Dust grains in the disc collided and stuck together, **accreting** into lumps, then rocks, then planets.
4. Close to the hot young Sun only rocky/metallic material could survive — building the rocky inner planets; further out, lighter gases and ices condensed, building the gas giants. The young Sun's radiation also drove the lightest gases outwards.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Order of planets outwards: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars | Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
• The model explains BOTH the composition split (rocky inside, gaseous outside) and why everything orbits in the same direction — the whole system inherited the spin of the original cloud.

notes.heading: Gravity, Weight and Light-Travel Time
notes.body:
📌 Definitions
**Gravitational field strength** $g$ is the force per kilogram on a mass at a point, in N/kg. **Weight** is the force of gravity on a mass: $W = mg$.

🔑 How it works — gravity varies between planets
The gravitational field strength at the surface of a planet depends on the **mass of the planet** (and how its mass is distributed): more massive planets have stronger surface fields. On the Moon $g \approx 1.6\text{ N/kg}$, on Earth $g \approx 9.8\text{ N/kg}$, on Jupiter $g \approx 25\text{ N/kg}$. The field around a planet also **decreases with distance** from it. Your MASS is the same everywhere; your WEIGHT changes with $g$.

💡 Worked Example
A $60\text{ kg}$ astronaut weighs $W = 60 \times 9.8 = 588\text{ N}$ on Earth. On Mars ($g = 3.7\text{ N/kg}$) the same astronaut weighs $60 \times 3.7 = 222\text{ N}$ — the mass is still $60\text{ kg}$.

🔑 How it works — light-travel time
Light is fast but not instantaneous: $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8}\text{ m/s}$. The time for light to cross space is $t = \dfrac{d}{c}$. Sunlight takes about **500 seconds (8 minutes)** to cross the $1.5 \times 10^{11}\text{ m}$ from the Sun to Earth — we always see the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago. Light from the next nearest star takes over 4 years.

💡 Worked Example
The Moon is $3.84 \times 10^{8}\text{ m}$ away. A laser pulse bounced off the Moon returns after $\dfrac{2 \times 3.84 \times 10^{8}}{3.0 \times 10^{8}} = 2.56\text{ s}$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Weight changes with the planet; mass never does.
• Light-travel time is an ordinary $t = \dfrac{d}{v}$ calculation with $v = c$ — watch for round trips.

notes.heading: Orbital Motion (Supplement)
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
The planets orbit the Sun because of its **gravitational attraction** — gravity continually pulls them inwards, bending their paths into orbits. For a circular orbit of radius $r$ completed in time $T$ (the period), the orbital speed is the circumference over the period:

$$v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$$

💡 Worked Example
Earth orbits at $r = 1.5 \times 10^{11}\text{ m}$ with $T = 1$ year $= 3.16 \times 10^{7}\text{ s}$. $v = \dfrac{2\pi \times 1.5 \times 10^{11}}{3.16 \times 10^{7}} = 3.0 \times 10^{4}\text{ m/s}$ — Earth races around the Sun at about $30\text{ km/s}$.

🔑 Interpreting planetary data
From a table of orbital radius and period you can deduce: **the further a planet is from the Sun, the slower it moves and the longer its year** (Mercury: 88 days; Neptune: 165 years). This is exactly what $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$ applied to the data shows, and it happens because gravity is weaker further from the Sun, so a slower speed suffices to keep the planet in orbit.

🔑 Elliptical orbits and energy
Orbits are slightly **elliptical**, not perfectly circular. A planet on an elliptical orbit moves **fastest when closest to the Sun and slowest when furthest away**. The energy argument: falling closer to the Sun, the planet LOSES gravitational potential energy and gains kinetic energy — so it speeds up. Climbing away, kinetic converts back to potential — it slows down. The total energy stays constant.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting that gravity itself supplies the inward pull — nothing "pushes" a planet forwards. Without the Sun's gravitational attraction a planet would simply carry on in a straight line.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$ — distance round the circle over time for one orbit; convert the period to seconds FIRST.
• Faster near, slower far — and say it with energy, not just as a fact.

notes.heading: Stars and Their Life Cycle (Supplement)
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A star is a ball of mostly hydrogen and helium that radiates energy released by the **nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium** in its core. Distances between stars are measured in **light-years**: one light-year is the distance light travels in one year,

$$1\text{ light-year} = 9.5 \times 10^{15}\text{ m}$$

(from $c \times 1\text{ year} = 3.0 \times 10^{8} \times 3.16 \times 10^{7}\text{ m}$). Galaxies each contain many billions of stars; the Sun is one star in the Milky Way, which is one of many billions of galaxies in the Universe.

🔑 How it works — the life cycle
1. **Protostar**: a nebula collapses under gravity and heats up.
2. **Main sequence**: fusion of hydrogen begins. The star is STABLE because the inward pull of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from the hot gas and radiation. The Sun is about halfway through its main-sequence life.
3. When the hydrogen runs low, a Sun-sized star swells into a **red giant**, then sheds its outer layers as a **planetary nebula**, leaving a hot, dense **white dwarf** that slowly cools and fades.
4. A much more massive star becomes a **red supergiant**, then explodes as a **supernova**, leaving a **neutron star** — or, if massive enough, a **black hole**.

🔑 Where elements come from
Fusion in stars builds elements up to iron; the **heavier-than-iron elements are formed in a supernova**. The debris from planetary nebulae and supernovae is scattered into space and recycled into later stars and planets — the atoms in the Solar System were made inside earlier stars.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Mass decides the path: Sun-like → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf; massive → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.
• A planetary nebula is expelled gas — nothing to do with planets forming.

notes.heading: The Big Bang: Redshift, CMBR and Hubble's Law (Supplement)
notes.body:
📌 Redshift — galaxies are receding
Light from a distant galaxy shows the same pattern of spectral lines as light from elements on Earth, but shifted towards **longer wavelengths** — the red end of the spectrum. This **redshift** means the galaxy is **moving away from us**: the waves are stretched as the source recedes. Observations show that **the more distant the galaxy, the greater the redshift** — so the more distant the galaxy, the faster it recedes. This is evidence that the Universe is expanding.

🔑 Hubble's law
Recession speed is proportional to distance:

$$v = H_0 d$$

with the **Hubble constant** $H_0 \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-18}\text{ s}^{-1}$.

💡 Worked Example
A galaxy at $d = 2.0 \times 10^{25}\text{ m}$ recedes at $v = 2.2 \times 10^{-18} \times 2.0 \times 10^{25} = 4.4 \times 10^{7}\text{ m/s}$.

🔑 Estimating the age of the Universe
If galaxies have always moved apart at their present rates, the time since everything was together is $\dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{1}{H_0}$:

$$\text{age} \approx \dfrac{1}{H_0} = \dfrac{1}{2.2 \times 10^{-18}}\text{ s} \approx 4.5 \times 10^{17}\text{ s} \approx 14\text{ billion years}$$

🔑 The cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR)
The **CMBR** is microwave radiation detected coming uniformly from **all directions** in space. It is the afterglow of the hot, dense early Universe, stretched by the expansion into microwaves. Its existence — predicted before it was found — is strong evidence for the **Big Bang**: the Universe began hot and dense and has been expanding and cooling ever since. Measurements of the brightness of distant **supernovae** extend the redshift–distance evidence to the furthest galaxies.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Redshift → receding; bigger redshift → further and faster.
• $v = H_0 d$ and age $\approx \dfrac{1}{H_0}$ are the two equations to use.
• CMBR = relic microwave glow of the early Universe, observed in every direction.

illustration.alt: A graph of recession speed against distance for galaxies: a straight line through the origin with slope H-nought, with example galaxies at twice the distance receding twice as fast.
illustration.caption: Hubble's law: recession speed is proportional to distance, v = H0d; 1/H0 estimates the age of the Universe.

flashcards.definition: Caused by the Earth rotating on its axis once in approximately 24 hours; each place faces the Sun (day) then away (night).
flashcards.example: The Sun appears to cross the sky daily because the Earth spins, not because the Sun orbits us.

flashcards.definition: Earth orbits the Sun in approximately 365 days. Seasons result from the tilt of Earth's axis: the hemisphere tilted towards the Sun gets more direct sunlight and longer days (summer).
flashcards.example: When the northern hemisphere has summer, the southern has winter.

flashcards.definition: Earth's natural satellite, orbiting about once a month and shining by reflected sunlight; its phases are our changing view of its sunlit half.
flashcards.example: A full cycle from new Moon to new Moon takes about a month.

flashcards.definition: The Solar System formed from a collapsing nebula: the centre became the protostar (Sun), the rest flattened into an accretion disc, and dust grains collided and stuck together to build the planets.
flashcards.example: Rocky planets formed near the hot young Sun; gas giants formed further out where gases and ices survived.

flashcards.definition: Force per kilogram at a point (N/kg); W = mg. Surface g depends on the planet's mass, and the field decreases with distance from the planet.
flashcards.example: g ≈ 9.8 N/kg on Earth but ≈ 3.7 N/kg on Mars, so the same mass weighs less on Mars.

flashcards.term: Mass vs weight in space physics
flashcards.definition: Mass (kg) is the amount of matter and is the same everywhere; weight (N) is the gravitational force on it and changes with g.
flashcards.example: A 60 kg astronaut weighs 588 N on Earth and 222 N on Mars, with 60 kg of mass in both places.

flashcards.definition: t = d/c with c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s; light from the Sun takes about 500 s (8 minutes) to reach Earth.
flashcards.example: We see the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago, and distant stars as they were years ago.

flashcards.definition: The distance light travels in one year: 9.5×10¹⁵ m. A unit of distance, not time.
flashcards.example: The nearest star beyond the Sun is just over 4 light-years away.

flashcards.definition: For a circular orbit, v = 2πr/T — circumference divided by period (convert T to seconds). Planets further from the Sun move slower.

Protostar → main sequence (gravity balanced by outward pressure, hydrogen fusing) → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf; massive stars → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.
flashcards.example: Elements heavier than iron are formed in a supernova and scattered into space.

flashcards.definition: Spectral lines from distant galaxies are shifted to longer wavelengths, showing they are moving away; more distant galaxies have greater redshift, so they recede faster — evidence the Universe is expanding.
flashcards.example: The same hydrogen lines seen in a lab appear further towards the red in a distant galaxy's light.

flashcards.definition: v = H₀d with H₀ ≈ 2.2×10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹; the age of the Universe ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The CMBR — microwave radiation from all directions — is the afterglow of the hot early Universe.
flashcards.example: A galaxy 2.0×10²⁵ m away recedes at about 4.4×10⁷ m/s.

questions.stem: Day and night on Earth are caused by:
choices: The Earth rotating on its axis once every 24 hours
The Sun orbiting the Earth once a day
The Earth tilting towards the Moon
questions.explanation: The Earth spins on its axis in about 24 hours, so each point on the surface alternately faces the Sun (day) and faces away (night). The Sun's apparent daily motion across the sky is this rotation seen from the ground.

questions.stem: Approximately how long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
questions.explanation: One orbit of the Sun takes approximately 365 days — one year. The 24-hour figure is the rotation period that gives day and night.

questions.stem: The Sun is composed mostly of:
questions.explanation: The Sun, like most stars, is mostly hydrogen with a substantial fraction of helium; it shines by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core.

questions.stem: The spectral lines in light from a distant galaxy are shifted towards the red end of the spectrum, compared with the same lines measured in a laboratory. This tells us the galaxy is: (Supplement)
choices: Made entirely of red giant stars
questions.explanation: Redshift means the wavelengths are stretched, which happens when the source is receding. A shift towards the blue would indicate approach.

questions.stem: The Moon goes through one complete cycle of phases (new Moon to new Moon) in approximately:
questions.explanation: The Moon orbits the Earth about once a month, and the cycle of phases — our changing view of its sunlit half — takes the same time, about a month.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the formation of the Solar System according to the accretion model?
choices: Nebula → gravitational collapse → protostar with an accretion disc → dust grains collide and stick together to build planets
Planets formed first, then the Sun ignited between them
The Sun captured passing planets from deep space
A supernova compressed cold rocks directly into planets
questions.explanation: In the accretion model a rotating cloud of gas and dust collapses under gravity; the hot centre becomes the protostar, the remainder flattens into an accretion disc, and grains in the disc collide and accrete into larger and larger bodies, forming the planets.

questions.stem: On Mars the gravitational field strength is $3.7\text{ N/kg}$. What is the weight of a $60\text{ kg}$ astronaut standing on Mars?
questions.explanation: $W = mg = 60 \times 3.7 = 222\text{ N}$. The $588\text{ N}$ option is the astronaut's weight on Earth ($60 \times 9.8$); the mass stays $60\text{ kg}$ on both planets.

questions.stem: The Sun is $1.5 \times 10^{11}\text{ m}$ from the Earth and light travels at $3.0 \times 10^{8}\text{ m/s}$. How long does sunlight take to reach the Earth?
questions.explanation: $t = \dfrac{d}{c} = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{11}}{3.0 \times 10^{8}} = 500\text{ s}$, which is just over $8$ minutes — we always see the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago.

questions.stem: Taking the Earth's orbit as a circle of radius $1.5 \times 10^{11}\text{ m}$ with a period of $3.16 \times 10^{7}\text{ s}$, what is the Earth's orbital speed? (Supplement)
questions.explanation: $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 1.5 \times 10^{11}}{3.16 \times 10^{7}} \approx 3.0 \times 10^{4}\text{ m/s} = 30\text{ km/s}$. The circumference is huge but so is a year, and they divide out to tens of kilometres per second.

questions.stem: One light-year, the distance light travels in one year, is approximately: (Supplement)
questions.explanation: Multiply the speed of light by the number of seconds in a year: $3.0 \times 10^{8} \times 3.16 \times 10^{7} \approx 9.5 \times 10^{15}\text{ m}$. The $3.0 \times 10^{8}$ option is the speed, not a distance; $1.5 \times 10^{11}\text{ m}$ is the Sun–Earth distance.

questions.stem: A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius $8.0 \times 10^{6}\text{ m}$ with a period of $8.0 \times 10^{3}\text{ s}$. What is its orbital speed? (Supplement)
questions.explanation: $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 8.0 \times 10^{6}}{8.0 \times 10^{3}} = 2\pi \times 1000 \approx 6.3 \times 10^{3}\text{ m/s}$. The $1.0 \times 10^{3}$ option forgets the factor of $2\pi$.

questions.stem: A planet follows an elliptical orbit around the Sun. Where does it move fastest, and why? (Supplement)
choices: At a constant speed all round, because gravity never changes
Fastest when closest to the Sun — gravitational potential energy converts to kinetic energy as it falls inwards
Fastest when furthest from the Sun, because gravity is weakest there
Slowest when closest to the Sun, because the Sun's gravity brakes it
questions.explanation: As the planet falls closer to the Sun it loses gravitational potential energy and gains kinetic energy, so it speeds up; climbing away again the conversion reverses and it slows. Total energy is conserved — the speed change is the energy conversion.

questions.stem: A distant galaxy is $2.0 \times 10^{25}\text{ m}$ away. Taking $H_0 = 2.2 \times 10^{-18}\text{ s}^{-1}$, what is its recession speed? (Supplement)
questions.explanation: Hubble's law: $v = H_0 d = 2.2 \times 10^{-18} \times 2.0 \times 10^{25} = 4.4 \times 10^{7}\text{ m/s}$ — about a seventh of the speed of light, which is why such galaxies show large redshifts.

questions.stem: Using $H_0 = 2.2 \times 10^{-18}\text{ s}^{-1}$, the estimate $\dfrac{1}{H_0}$ for the age of the Universe gives approximately: (Supplement)
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{1}{H_0} = \dfrac{1}{2.2 \times 10^{-18}} = 4.5 \times 10^{17}\text{ s}$, and dividing by the $3.16 \times 10^{7}$ seconds in a year gives $1.4 \times 10^{10}$ years — about $14$ billion years.

questions.stem: For a star much more massive than the Sun, which sequence follows its main-sequence stage? (Supplement)
choices: Red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
Red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
Straight from the main sequence to a black hole
questions.explanation: Massive stars swell into red supergiants, then explode as supernovae — forming elements heavier than iron — leaving a neutron star or, for the most massive, a black hole. The red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf path is for Sun-sized stars.
